reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-three home runs projected at age 23, and the Statcast profile says believe it. His 93.0 mph average exit velocity sits in the 96th percentile, and he's barreling the ball at 13.0% while walking at 11.8%, so the .892 OPS projection is built on contact quality and strike zone command, not a hot stretch. The one real drag is defense, with an OAA percentile at 1, meaning Tampa has to decide how long third base stays the answer before the bat carries him somewhere else. If that glove costs him the position, the profile becomes a DH question, and the value shifts from "cornerstone" to "cornerstone bat in search of a home."

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The tension in this profile is the gap between a 26.1% strikeout rate and a .359 xwOBA, both real, both pulling in opposite directions. Crow-Armstrong's 12.4% barrel rate and 48.3% hard-hit rate say the contact quality is genuine when he gets to pitches; his 34.2% chase rate says he's going to miss enough that the .250 xBA isn't hiding anything. The projection at .272/.366/.537 is essentially betting that a 12.0% walk rate keeps the strikeouts from eating the slash line, which is a reasonable bet if the plate discipline holds at that level. If the chase rate climbs and the walks dry up, this becomes a power-first profile carried by 39 home runs and 39 stolen bags, still a very good player, just a thinner one.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .303, 100th percentile, and the xSLG at .506, and neither number needs defending — 51.3% hard contact at 92.5 mph average exit velocity is a profile that produces those outcomes almost mechanically. The one honest friction point is a 33.1% chase rate that slots in the bottom quarter of the league, which means he's generating elite contact quality despite undisciplined pitch selection, not because of clean zone management. If pitchers ever solve him with something that exploits that chase tendency systematically, the projection's .288/.363/.466 gets squeezed from the average side before it gets squeezed from the power side. He won't be solved that way, though, because 30.1 ft/s sprint speed means that even a contact dip doesn't crater the batting average the way it would for a slower slugger, and 42 projected steals give him a run-contribution floor that holds up across bad stretches.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The Statcast batting profile is essentially a ceiling argument all by itself: .407 xwOBA, 16.6% barrel rate, 93.5 mph average exit velocity, all clustering at the very top of the sport. The one friction point is contact quality against swing decisions — a 30.7% whiff rate sits at the 14th percentile, meaning pitchers can expand the zone and find swings and misses, but his 13.6% walk rate shows he also knows when not to chase. On the mound, a 2.72 xERA and 30.4% whiff rate as a pitcher describe a genuine frontline arm, not a novelty, and the projection of 38 home runs with a .935 OPS across 692 plate appearances is simply what he does when healthy. The whole profile hinges on staying on the field as a pitcher; the hitting is close to a given.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The bat-to-ball profile is genuinely worrying, but the contact quality is exceptional enough that it almost doesn't matter. Walker's 92.5 mph average exit velocity and 13.7% barrel rate sit well above the median, and his .355 xwOBA reflects that the damage he does when he makes contact is sustained across a full season of Statcast data. The problem is the 35.8% chase rate and 30.6% whiff rate, both near the bottom of the league, meaning pitchers with a plan can bury him outside the zone and wait. If he cleans up the chase rate even modestly, a .281/.339/.491 line with 32 home runs and 21 steals is the outcome; if he doesn't, the K% swells and the counting stats erode from there.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The xSLG sitting at .475 with a 13.2% barrel rate is the spine of this profile, contact quality that earns the power rather than borrowing it from a friendly park or a hot month. Stewart's xwOBA of .349 runs well ahead of his xBA of .256, which is exactly what a corner bat built on loft looks like at 22: the value lives in the slugging, not the hit tool. A 27.0% whiff rate and 30.5% chase rate are both ordinary, neither disqualifying nor reassuring, and they're the one thing standing between a solid regular and something more. The projection at 34 home runs and a .806 OPS over 704 plate appearances is where this lands if the barrel rate travels, and at his age, there's room to close the gap.

reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
reports.published_report: The contact quality here is almost unfair: a 54.0% hard-hit rate and an xBA of .298 say the hits are coming whether pitchers like it or not. His 26.9% whiff rate looks alarming until you see the 18.3% strikeout rate — he's making enough contact on the pitches he offers at to keep the swing-and-miss from eating into his production. Built out to 710 projection plate appearances, that translates to a .286/.358/.457 hitter with 23 home runs and 36 stolen bases, a five-category engine who costs you almost nothing in batting average or on-base to run. The profile hinges entirely on health; give him the full season and the counting stats take care of themselves.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The power-speed combination is legitimate, but the plate discipline is the ceiling cap. Merrill's .463 xSLG and 46.6% hard-hit rate show genuine thump, and 29.0 ft/s sprint speed puts him in rare company on the bases, yet a 37.4% chase rate with a 6.2% walk rate means pitchers can shrink the zone and win. The projection, 26 home runs, 27 steals, .706 OPS across 667 plate appearances, reflects exactly that tension: a player whose contact quality outpaces his contact rates, landing him in solid-regular territory rather than star territory. If the chase rate comes down even modestly, the .463 xSLG has room to actually show up in the slash line; if it doesn't, he's a productive, occasionally maddening everyday outfielder who gives you counting stats while leaving on-base percentage stranded at .290.

reports.name: Yordan Alvarez
reports.published_report: A .458 xwOBA at the 100th percentile, an xSLG of .673, and a 16.0% walk rate that ranks with the game's most patient hitters — the Statcast profile doesn't leave much room for debate. reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The exit velocity tells you what he is: 93.9 mph average, 98th percentile, with a 51.3% hard-hit rate that explains why his xwOBA sits at .360 even while he strikes out 27.5% of the time. The whiff rate is the tax on the power, and it's a steep one, but a 10.6% walk rate keeps the damage from compounding. Everything hinges on whether that contact quality holds as pitchers continue to map his zone, because if the chase rate climbs past its current 26.0%, the strikeout problem stops being manageable and starts eating the projected .340 OBP. He's a legitimate 26-HR, 29-SB shortstop with a .811 OPS if the discipline stays where it is now, and that's a star profile at a premium position.

reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: The xwOBA and xSLG sit comfortably above league average, .338 and .440, for a shortstop projecting at 34 home runs and 32 stolen bases across 667 plate appearances. Sprint speed at the 81st percentile gives the stolen base number a believable foundation; the barrel rate at 10.1% explains how the power translates even without elite exit velocity. The problem is a 37.0% chase rate that lands in the 14th percentile, giving pitchers a repeatable blueprint, which is why the expected numbers run ahead of the contact ones and why this entire profile depends on whether he can tighten his zone decisions enough to stop handing that blueprint back every at-bat. If he can't, the .272 average softens and 8.7% walks don't cover the gap.

reports.name: Corbin Carroll
reports.published_report: The contact piece is where this profile wobbles, and the rest of it is genuinely loud. A 27.1% whiff rate drags against an 11.8% walk rate and 49.0% hard-hit rate that both sit well above the middle of the league, and the result is an xwOBA of .349 that the projection's .835 OPS mostly reflects. Carroll hits the ball hard enough to carry the strikeouts, and the 29.7 ft/s sprint speed at the 97th percentile means he earns bases even when he doesn't barrel it. The profile hinges on whether the whiff stays manageable rather than drifting upward — if contact erodes, the power and speed still leave an interesting player, but the .252/.348/.487 line shrinks toward something you can live with rather than something you build around.

reports.name: Kevin McGonigle
reports.published_report: The discipline here is genuinely unusual: a 19.4% chase rate that grades at the 98th percentile, matched exactly by a 13.7% walk rate and a 13.7% strikeout rate, which is a combination you almost never see at 22. The underlying contact quality is the tension — a .353 xwOBA with an average exit velocity of 88.2 mph suggests he's finding barrels through placement and approach rather than raw thump, and the .434 xSLG says the power projection of 18 home runs is backed by contact shape even if the hard-hit rate at 37.1% doesn't scream plus raw power. If pitchers find a way to exploit the zone against a hitter this passive about swinging at balls, the walk rate compresses and the whole profile gets thinner. But if the zone management holds, he's a .279/.378 everyday infielder with 14 stolen bases and 101 runs, and that's a legitimate building block for Detroit at 22.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: Gunnar Henderson

What keeps this from being a shrug is the 44.8% hard-hit rate, which sits well above where the barrel numbers would suggest, and the projection's 25 home runs across 721 plate appearances shows the power translating despite the modest expected-slugging figure. The whole read hinges on whether the .226 projected average reflects real contact suppression or a BABIP correction that's overcooking — at a 22.1% strikeout rate with average chase and whiff numbers, there's nothing in the profile that demands the bat-to-ball be this limited, so if the average creeps toward that .244 xBA, the .712 OPS projection looks like a floor rather than a ceiling for an everyday shortstop with above-average speed and a 71st-percentile glove.

reports.name: Cam Schlittler

His xERA sits at 2.92 and his xwOBA at .266, both backed by a 98.0 mph fastball with 2527 rpm of spin — that's a combination that explains why the swings-and-misses come without needing to chase barrels down. reports.name: Zach Neto
reports.published_report: The barrel rate is the argument. The projection, 27 home runs across 708 plate appearances with a .431 slugging mark, is a portrait of a player whose ceiling is tied directly to his own swing decisions. If the chase rate doesn't come down, the strikeouts stay near 30.7% and the batting average stays thin, and what you have is a shortstop who hits for power in chunks but bleeds outs between them.

reports.name: Tyler Bremner
reports.published_report: The K-BB% is the loud number here: 23% across AA & A+, sitting at the 95th percentile in its pool. Bremner is striking out 84 batters across 63.3 innings while walking only 23, and the separation between those two rates is what gives the command story some credibility even with a 4.3 ERA and a 1.3 WHIP suggesting the results aren't yet clean. The MLB-equivalent translation puts his K-BB% at 14.3%, his walk rate a shade worse than the majors absorb comfortably, and that gap is exactly what the profile hinges on — if the walks tick up as competition sharpens, the ceiling compresses from back-end starter toward a bullpen role. The strikeout rate translates to 8.9 K/9, roughly where big-league pitching runs, which means the margin for error on the command side is thinner than the minor-league line makes it look.

reports.name: Luis García Jr.
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is elite from the elbows down and a problem from the eyes up. García's xSLG sits at .506 and his xBA at .288, both sitting at or above the 94th percentile, so the raw contact quality is genuine and the projection's .542 SLG isn't chasing ghosts. But a 38.6% chase rate puts him near the bottom of the league, and a 4.9% walk rate follows naturally from that, which caps the ceiling on an otherwise loud bat. If pitchers keep attacking him with breaking stuff away and he keeps biting, the .316 OBP on a 32-homer profile stays just good enough rather than great, and that's the whole tension: he's a middle-of-the-order force if the contact quality carries the day, and a streaky cleanup hitter with a real vulnerability if the zone-judgment gap gets exploited in October counts.

reports.name: Bo Bichette
reports.published_report: The .279 xBA sits in the 89th percentile while the walk rate is near the bottom of the league — that's the whole tension in this profile. Bichette makes elite contact, routinely puts the ball in play at quality rates, and his 19.3% whiff rate looks like a legitimate skill, but a 41.2% chase rate keeps the OBP floor low and the ceiling capped, and the projection reflects exactly that: a .314 OBP across 694 plate appearances tells you what happens when great bat-to-ball lives alongside almost no plate discipline. If the chase rate ever softens even modestly, there's a second-division regular who hits .270 with pop here; if it doesn't, he's already showing you what he is: a high-average, low-OBP shortstop whose value rides almost entirely on his ability to make contact with pitches most hitters leave alone.

reports.published_report: A 12.7% strikeout rate that grades in the 91st percentile tells you most of what you need to know: Lopez makes contact at a level that almost no one in the league matches, and his .281 xBA backs that up by sitting in the same tier. reports.name: Hunter Goodman
reports.published_report: Thirty-nine projected home runs from a catcher is the whole argument, and the Statcast profile explains exactly how it's possible: a 16.9% barrel rate sitting in the 98th percentile, with an xSLG of .472 to back the contact quality. The problem is just as visible — a 33.0% strikeout rate at the 2nd percentile and a 40.2% chase rate at the 5th percentile, and those aren't quirks you discipline away, they're the shape of the swing. Colorado's park inflates the projection ceiling here, so the real question is whether the bat-to-ball issues, compounded by a 35.6% whiff rate, get exploited enough to crater the xwOBA below its current .331 once pitchers have a full book on him. If the power translates and the strikeouts stay manageable, he's a viable everyday catcher with genuine thump; if pitchers go after his chase habits and the K rate climbs further, what's left is a platoon bat who hits the ball hard when he connects.

reports.name: Rainiel Rodriguez
reports.published_report:
.322/.406/.573 at 19 years old, catching, across AA & A+. That line does most of the talking.

reports.name: Payton Tolle

What makes it credible is the chase rate: 35.7% gets hitters fishing out of the zone at a frequency that suppresses hard contact even when the whiff rate inside the zone is ordinary. The 27.9% strikeout rate and 6.9% walk rate are genuinely useful, not spectacular, so the ERA gap between 2.70 and the projection's 3.22 across 157.3 innings is probably the honest range, with the outcome depending almost entirely on whether that chase rate holds at full-season depth against lineups seeing him multiple times. If it does, he's a front-end arm for Boston. If the chase rate regresses and the zone stuff doesn't compensate, you're looking at a perfectly solid mid-rotation innings-eater — which, on a 10-win, 14-quality-start projection, isn't nothing.

If he finds the zone, back-end starter is a real destination; if the walks follow him up the system, what's left is a depth arm.

The walk rate at 8.2% is the quiet drag on the profile, sitting below average, which is why the .337 OBP on a .271 projection line looks about right rather than generous. If the contact shape holds, he's a useful everyday outfielder for a Dodgers lineup that can absorb the pedestrian walk rate; if the batted-ball distribution regresses toward what 88.8 mph typically produces, the .795 OPS projection starts to feel like a ceiling rather than a center.

reports.name: Seth Hernandez
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest thing on the page, and the walk rate is the thing you have to watch. Across A+ & A in 2026, Seth Hernandez has struck out 118 batters in 74 innings, 14.3 per nine, with a K-BB% of 30 that sits in the 99th percentile of his pool, and a 2.4 ERA with a 1.1 WHIP. Back-end starter if it comes together; depth arm if it doesn't.

reports.name: Jeremy Peña
reports.published_report: The .277 xBA sitting in the 86th percentile while his exit velocity ranks 36th tells you exactly what Peña is: a contact manipulator, not a masher, and one who chases far too much for the discipline numbers to ever look clean. His 37.4% chase rate and 30.9% whiff rate are genuinely damaging, yet the batted-ball profile finds enough barrel to project 19 home runs because he makes loud contact when he connects. The read hinges entirely on his 29.2 ft/s sprint speed, which is a genuine asset that inflates his average and stolen base line in ways the raw exit velocity alone would never suggest. If the chase rate climbs further, the hit tool erodes and you're left with a shortstop hitting .255 with modest pop, which is a very different player than the .281-.798 OPS projection implies.

The xERA is 2.51, the xwOBA .247, and both percentile out at 96, meaning hitters are genuinely helpless against him rather than just unlucky. The 11.0% walk rate is the complication, the one number that keeps the stuff from translating cleanly, and if he can't tighten the zone, those free baserunners will eventually find a way to cost him. But with 100.6 mph on the fastball, a 29.8% whiff rate, and a projected 3.07 ERA across 64.5 innings of high-leverage work for the Dodgers, the gap between what he is and what the ERA says is mostly the walks. Solve that and he's a genuine shutdown piece.

reports.name: Justin Wrobleski
reports.published_report: The 3.62 ERA projection is doing a lot of heavy lifting against a 4.66 xERA, and the Statcast contact profile explains why that gap is uncomfortable. A 43.9% hard-hit rate and 90.0 mph average exit velocity are bottom-fifth marks, meaning hitters are squaring him up regularly, and a 20.0% whiff rate offers almost no escape valve. The one genuine skill is command: a 5.4% walk rate in the 93rd percentile is the real thing, and it keeps him functional in a rotation where control alone can generate quality starts. If that walk rate slips and he's still giving up hard contact without missing bats, there's not much floor left — what remains is a back-end arm whose survival depends almost entirely on not beating himself.

reports.name: Jacob Berry
reports.published_report: The profile lives and dies on plate discipline: 49 walks against 55 strikeouts across 350 AAA plate appearances in 2026, and that shape translates to an 11.3% walk rate at the MLB level where the average hitter barely clears 8.5%. That contact-and-patience foundation gets him to a .364 OBP at AAA, but the power isn't there to carry a corner outfield profile, with an MLB-equivalent ISO of .129 while the typical big leaguer sits at .150. Baker's .269 xwOBA and 2.98 xERA tell the same story: hitters aren't squaring him up, and the 44 projected saves suggest Tampa is leaning into that heavily. The walk rate at 7.8% is the one lever that could loosen this whole thing — if command slips and he loses the ability to attack the zone, the chase numbers mean less because he's not putting hitters in bad counts to begin with. Clean profile, real closer usage, with the caveat that his margin for error narrows fast if the command drifts.

reports.name: Byron Buxton
reports.published_report: The barrel rate tells you everything you need to know about why 31 projected home runs is believable at 32 years old: 15.9% puts him in the 96th percentile, and an xSLG of .488 confirms the damage is there when he makes contact. The problem is getting to the ball in the first place — a 34.4% chase rate and 31.3% whiff rate are bottom-of-the-league territory, which is why his xBA sits at .248 even with all that raw power. The whole profile hinges on plate appearances; at 523 projected, he's already being penciled in for near-full health, and the gap between what he does when he plays and what the season line looks like depends entirely on his body holding up across that full workload. If it does, the .823 OPS projection is conservative given the contact quality. If it doesn't, you're back to the same conversation you've been having about Buxton for six years.

Thompson's contact and patience translate to a 19.3% strikeout rate and 14.1% walk rate against the MLB average, which means the plate discipline isn't a AAA mirage, it's a genuine skill. The power is a different conversation: his .147 ISO equivalent sits right at the MLB mean, and with a .376 BABIP propping the raw line, the hit tool has to stay sharp for any of this to hold at the next level. reports.published_report: The ratios are loud. A 27% K-BB% at AA with a 2.5 BB/9 is an unusually clean control profile for a level where most arms are still negotiating the strike zone. Across AA & A+, the MLB translation puts his K-BB% at 15.8% against a 13.5% MLB baseline, and his walk rate lands just below 3.2. The catch is 42.7 innings, a prior-season sample, and a ceiling that doesn't stretch past depth arm — if the control holds in a larger upper-level stint, he's a functional big-league reliever; if it doesn't, the ERA and WHIP figures here become a small-sample number and the profile shrinks to organizational depth.

reports.name: Robert Arias
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk combination at A-ball is genuinely unusual for a 19-year-old: 14% strikeouts, 15% walks, a .397 OBP across 190 plate appearances in 2026. That discipline translates to a 20.6% K rate and 10.2% BB rate in MLB-equivalent terms, both better than the average big leaguer, which is the part of this profile worth keeping. The power is where the ceiling closes — a .171 ISO at A is fine, but it translates to .127 against big-league pitching, well below the MLB mean, and the 5 home runs in 190 PA don't suggest that gap narrows on its own. If the speed (21 stolen bases at A) plays in center and the bat-to-ball holds as competition rises, there's a path to an everyday-ish role built on contact and baserunning; if the game power never develops, what's left is a bench piece who gets on base.

reports.name: Tekoah Roby
reports.published_report: The control is what makes this profile worth a second look. Across 47 innings at AA, Roby posted a 2.1 BB/9 and a 1.0 WHIP, and when that command translates to an MLB context across AAA & AA, the walk rate holds — 2.7 BB/9, comfortably better than the MLB average, with a K-BB% that lands at 15.1%. The strikeout rate is the asterisk: his K/9 translates to 8.5, essentially matching what an average MLB arm produces, which means the profile lives or dies on whether the command stays elite enough to compensate. If it does, he's a useful depth piece who earns a rotation spot in a pinch; if the stuff doesn't miss enough bats against better competition, he settles into a bullpen role where the control still plays.

reports.published_report: A 1.90 ERA and a 0.90 WHIP across 29 AAA innings would be the whole conversation if Snelling weren't sitting on the 60-day IL right now. His K-BB% at AAA ranks 97th in the pitcher pool, and the strikeout rate translates to 9.9 per nine at the MLB level, well clear of the MLB average of 8.6. The walk rate is the one honest wrinkle: 15 free passes in 29 AAA innings translates to 3.8 per nine in the majors, a little loose for a rotation piece, and that's what the floor hinges on. If the IL stint is short and the command firms up, he's more than a depth arm; if the walks don't tighten, that depth ceiling is probably where he lands.

reports.name: Drew Cavanaugh
reports.published_report: The .449 OBP across AAA & AA is doing a lot of work here, and the BABIP of .401 is doing most of the heavy lifting behind it. Cavanaugh has 35 walks against 55 strikeouts in 227 plate appearances, which translates to an 11.4% walk rate when moved to an MLB context, comfortably above the 8.5% MLB baseline. The MLB-equivalent ISO comes out to .170, just nudging past that same baseline figure of .150, which is fine for a catcher but not the kind of carrying tool that survives a BABIP correction. If the average regresses hard and the power stays modest, you're left with a patient backstop who can work counts at the margin, which is a bench catcher, not a regular.

reports.name: Brady Smith
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and the translation is where it gets complicated. Across A+ & A, Brady Smith is punching out hitters at 13.2 per nine over 80.7 innings, 118 strikeouts against 34 walks, and that K-BB% sits in the 94th percentile of the pitcher pool. The problem is that when you run the MLB-equivalent translation, the strikeouts flatten to 8.7 per nine, essentially league average, and the walks translate to 4.2 against a translated K-BB% of 13.1 percent where the MLB average sits at 13.5, meaning the dominant shape at the lower levels becomes a break-even profile one level at a time. The whole case hinges on whether the swing-and-miss travels up the ladder or belongs to the level.

reports.name: Jadher Areinamo
reports.published_report: The power profile at AA is the most interesting thing here, and also the thing that shrinks the most on translation. A .189 ISO across 293 PA at AA reads well on the card, but the MLB-equivalent drops to .146, roughly what a league-average bat produces, and the walk rate translates to 6.6% against a baseline that most big-league regulars clear comfortably. The contact side is quieter than the raw line suggests: a .277 BABIP holding up a .256 average, with 57 strikeouts kept manageable but an OBP of .302 that leaves almost no margin. If the power stays near that translated floor and the walk rate doesn't grow, what's left is a middle-infield profile that fits a bench role more than a lineup spot.

reports.name: Andrew Pintar
reports.published_report: The 27 stolen bases at AAA are the loudest thing on this card, and the rest of the profile tells you exactly why that matters more than the power. The MLB-equivalent translation puts his ISO at .133, a step below what an average big-league bat produces, so the gap-to-gap game isn't going to carry him; what keeps him relevant is the contact rate and the legs, a .266/.356 line in 364 AAA plate appearances built on 41 walks and a strikeout rate that translates just a tick above big-league norms. This profile hinges entirely on whether the speed plays at the next level, because if it doesn't, you're left with a below-average power bat and a walk rate that lands near the middle of the pack. Bench outfielder with a real path to a specific role if a team values defense and baserunning; organizational depth if they don't.
